title: Revocation, dev certs and mutual TLS
summary: How a certificate is cancelled before it expires, why dev certs need trusting, and what changes when the client shows a certificate too.

steps.title: Revocation: cancelling a certificate early
body: If a private key leaks, the certificate is still in date and still chains. The CA must **revoke** it, and clients must find out.
- **CRL** (Certificate Revocation List): a file, signed by the CA, listing revoked serial numbers. Its URL is in the certificate's
*CRL Distribution Points* extension. Clients download and cache it.
- **OCSP**: ask the CA's responder "is serial X still good?" and get a signed yes/no. The URL is in *Authority Information Access*.
- **OCSP stapling**: the *server* fetches the signed OCSP answer and sends it in the handshake, so clients don't have to call the CA.
In .NET: `ChainPolicy.RevocationMode` is `Online` (fetch), `Offline` (cache only) or `NoCheck`. If the CRL/OCSP server can't be reached you get
`RevocationStatusUnknown` / `OfflineRevocation`; a revoked certificate gives `Revoked`.
> **Tip:** Locked-down servers that can't reach the CA's CRL URL are a classic source of slow handshakes and
> `RevocationStatusUnknown`. Check the URL from the server with `certutil -url cert.cer`.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its description.
pairs: a signed list of revoked serial numbers
a live signed answer about one certificate
the server attaches a fresh OCSP answer to its handshake
the client couldn't find out either way
the CA has cancelled this certificate

steps.prompt: A service fails TLS only on production servers, which have no outbound internet. Errors mention `RevocationStatusUnknown` and `OfflineRevocation`. What is going on?
options: The servers can't reach the CA's CRL/OCSP URLs to check revocation
The root CA is untrusted on production
steps.explain: "Unknown" isn't "revoked". Allow the CRL/OCSP URLs through the firewall (or use a CA whose answers the server can staple). Don't fix it by switching revocation off everywhere.

steps.title: Self-signed dev certificates
body: `dotnet dev-certs https` creates a self-signed certificate for `localhost` and puts it in `Cert:\CurrentUser\My`.
Until you run `dotnet dev-certs https --trust`, browsers say `NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID`: the chain is just one
self-signed certificate, and it isn't in any trust store. `--trust` adds it to `Cert:\CurrentUser\Root`.
That trust is per machine and per user: your Docker container, your colleague's laptop and your CI agent don't have it.
The tempting "fix" is to switch validation off:
```csharp
handler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback = (_, _, _, _) => true;   // accepts ANY certificate
That accepts an attacker's certificate too, and it has a way of reaching production. Trust the specific root instead,
for example with a `CustomTrustStore` as you've been doing in this course.

steps.prompt: Which is the safest way to let a test client call a service whose certificate comes from your team's private test CA?
options: Validate against that CA's root explicitly (custom trust store or installing the root on the test machines)
Call the service over plain HTTP instead
steps.explain: Trusting one specific root keeps every other check (dates, names, the signature chain) working. Accept-all disables all of them.

steps.title: Mutual TLS: the client shows a certificate too
body: In normal TLS only the server proves who it is. In **mutual TLS (mTLS)** the server also asks the client for a certificate,
and the client proves it holds that certificate's private key.
| | Server certificate | Client certificate |
| Who validates it | the client | the server |
| EKU needed | serverAuth `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1` | clientAuth `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2` |
| Name check | hostname vs SAN | your own rule (Subject, SAN, or thumbprint allow-list) |
| Trusted roots | public roots, usually | usually **your own private CA**, not the public ones |
The server should trust *only* the CA that issues client certificates. If it trusted all public roots, anyone who bought a
certificate anywhere could connect. In .NET the client attaches one with `handler.ClientCertificates.Add(certWithKey)`.

steps.prompt: In mutual TLS, which side does each job?
items: checks the client certificate chains to the client CA
holds the private key for a clientAuth certificate
asks for a certificate during the handshake
holds the private key for a serverAuth certificate

steps.title: Accept a client certificate
prompt: You run an mTLS API. Write `bool AcceptClient(X509Certificate2 client, X509Certificate2 clientCaRoot, List<X509Certificate2> sent)`
that accepts the client only if:
- it chains to `clientCaRoot` **only** (custom root trust), with `sent` as extra certificates,
- it is valid for **client authentication** (`ApplicationPolicy` with OID `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2`),
- checked at `new DateTime(2031, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)` with revocation off (`NoCheck`; there's no CRL in the test).
starter: bool AcceptClient(X509Certificate2 client, X509Certificate2 clientCaRoot, List<X509Certificate2> sent)
solution: bool AcceptClient(X509Certificate2 client, X509Certificate2 clientCaRoot, List<X509Certificate2> sent)
hints: It's the `Validates` setup from module 2 plus one line.
template: using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates;
{{CODE}}
var dojoClientRoot = DojoCert("CN=Client Root", null, true);
var dojoClientCa = DojoCert("CN=Client Issuing CA", dojoClientRoot, true);
var dojoGood = DojoCert("CN=device-42", dojoClientCa, false, null, "1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2");
var dojoServerish = DojoCert("CN=device-43", dojoClientCa, false, null, "1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1");
var dojoPublicRoot = DojoCert("CN=Some Public Root", null, true);
var dojoStranger = DojoCert("CN=device-99", dojoPublicRoot, false, null, "1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2");
Dojo.Eq("a clientAuth certificate from our CA is accepted", true, AcceptClient(dojoGood, dojoClientRoot, new() { dojoClientCa }));
Dojo.Eq("a serverAuth-only certificate from our CA is refused", false, AcceptClient(dojoServerish, dojoClientRoot, new() { dojoClientCa }));
Dojo.Eq("a clientAuth certificate from another CA is refused", false, AcceptClient(dojoStranger, dojoClientRoot, new() { dojoPublicRoot }));
Dojo.Eq("missing the issuing CA is refused", false, AcceptClient(dojoGood, dojoClientRoot, new()));
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var key = ECDsa.Create(ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256);
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509BasicConstraintsExtension(isCa, false, 0, true));
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509SubjectKeyIdentifierExtension(req.PublicKey, false));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
var nb = new DateTimeOffset(nbYear, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
var na = new DateTimeOffset(naYear, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
if (issuer == null) return req.CreateSelfSigned(nb, na);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(X509AuthorityKeyIdentifierExtension.CreateFromCertificate(issuer, true, false));
var serial = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(8); serial[0] &= 0x7F;
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
return pub.CopyWithPrivateKey(key);
